name: Board
description: Records in columns by the stage they are at, where each column is one stage and moving a card between two of them is a state change on the server. The column header carries the count, and every move can be made from the keyboard.
when_to_use: A set of records where the stage is the thing being managed and the count per stage is a question somebody actually asks — an approval pipeline from Raised to Approved, a production board from Planned to QC, a QC hold board somebody clears before the shift ends. Both halves have to be true, and this is the layout that gets over-reached for, so start from the assumption that it is the wrong answer. A register with a status column is right far more often, and that is index-page: it sorts, filters, pages, exports, and gives the whole width to the columns being compared instead of a third of it to four stages nobody rebalances. A queue worked one record at a time is list-detail — a board shows forty cards and asks you to choose one, a queue hands you the next one and keeps the record beside it. Rows under stage subheadings is table's grouped variant, which is a board flattened: the same records and the same stages in a shape that reads down rather than across, prints in one pass, and holds fourteen columns of figures no card can carry. The board earns its place only when the horizontal split does work no vertical grouping can — when the split itself is being rebalanced, when how wide a stage has grown is the point, and when the move is a transaction rather than an edit. If nobody moves a card, this is a grouped register drawn sideways. Past about seven stages it stops working at any width and the answer is the register with a stage filter.
rules: Keyboard first, drag second, and the order is the component. The primary move is: reach a card, open its move control, choose a stage, and the card lands there. Drag is an accelerant layered over an interaction that already works without it — HTML5 drag events have no keyboard gesture anybody uses and do not fire on a touch screen at all, and this software is read on a tablet on the shop floor by somebody wearing gloves. A board whose only move is a drag is not a board with an accessibility gap in it; it is a board that half the people who need it cannot operate.

The stage list is a disclosure inside the card, not a menu anchored to it. Every column on a board is its own scroller and overflow-y-auto clips both axes, so an anchored panel is cut off by the column it opens in. dropdown's own answer to that is a fixed panel positioned from a measurement of the trigger, and such a panel has to close on scroll — on a board that scrolls in two axes while it is being read, closing on scroll shuts the panel the moment somebody looks for the column they are aiming at. A panel in normal flow inside the card cannot be clipped, is the same control at 390px as at 1440px, and gives 36px targets without a second layout.

A column is a plain ul role="list" and never a listbox. A card carries a link and a control, and a listbox is one Tab stop inside which nothing is reachable — that rule is list-detail's, and it is exactly what separates the two layouts. A queue whose rows are inert is a listbox; a board whose cards are operated is a list of ordinary elements.

The move is a server write, not a visual rearrangement, and the markup has to show the gap between the two. The card is placed in the destination optimistically, goes aria-busy with its move control aria-disabled while the request is in flight, and on a refusal returns to the column it came from carrying the reason the server gave. A board that moves the card and never reconciles is a board where the screen and the ledger disagree until somebody reloads.

Counts and totals are derived from the same array the cards render from, never held beside it. A count kept separately is wrong for the one second after a move when somebody is looking at it, which is the only second that matters. The board total is the sum across the columns and it does not change when a card moves — only the split does, and a board total that moves on a stage change is double counting.

The board region is the one place in this system where a horizontal scroll is correct, and it happens inside its own overflow-x-auto box rather than on the page. Columns are a fixed width and shrink-0: let them share the width instead and five stages give five 78px columns at 390px, none of which holds a record number. snap-x on the region and snap-start on the column means a swipe lands a whole column under the thumb rather than halfway between two.

A board card is not the card component. The column is the panel — rounded-xl, white, border-zinc-300 — and the cards inside it are rounded-lg on a bg-zinc-50 track, because a rounded-xl card inside a rounded-xl column is a card inside a card, which card's own entry calls a layout mistake.

The card carries no status pill. The column it is sitting in is its status, and a pill that repeats the column header is the first thing to delete from a board card. A pill on a different axis is another matter — a delivery that is overdue on a card in an approval column is real information, and that is what the exception line is for.

Focus after a move has to be put back by hand, and three things have to be right or it fails silently. The card is destroyed in one x-for and created in another, so the control that was just pressed no longer exists and focus has fallen to the body. The handler was called from inside the iteration being torn down, so it has to capture $refs.board into a local before it changes the stage — a deferred callback that reaches for this.$refs afterwards finds undefined, and the only symptom is that focus never moves. And the restore happens on the frame after the tick rather than in it, because at $nextTick the destination column has not been painted and the query finds either nothing or the node that is about to be removed. Take inline: "nearest" as well as block on the scrollIntoView, because the column the card landed in is often off the right edge.

Every column carries position: relative, and it is load-bearing rather than decorative. An absolutely positioned descendant is clipped by an ancestor scroller only when that ancestor is in its containing-block chain, so an sr-only span — position:absolute, one pixel, no positioned ancestor — resolves against the document and reports its static position from the fourth column, seven hundred pixels past the right edge of a phone. The board region clips it out of sight and the page still grows a horizontal scrollbar, which is the one thing this system does not allow. One relative on the column fixes every sr-only, tooltip anchor and absolute badge inside it at once.

The card is found again by an unquoted attribute selector, so every record number on a board has to be a valid CSS identifier. PO-2026-0418 and MS-4821 are; a number with a slash or a leading digit in it is not, and the query silently matches nothing.

Tab is the cost of the design. One link and one control per card is two stops, so a board of sixty cards is a hundred and twenty of them — which is why the filter bar is not decoration, why a card never carries a third control, and why the answer to a board somebody has to walk end to end is a filter rather than a longer board.

A stage over its limit is advisory and a stage that refuses is not, and they are drawn differently on purpose. Over the limit is an alert-triangle in amber-700 beside the count, and nothing else changes — no amber column, no field of colour. A stage that will not accept another card carries its destination button as aria-disabled with the reason written on the button, because a destination that has silently disappeared from the list is a board that looks broken.

The columns come from the stage list, not from the data. A stage with nothing in it still renders, with its header, its count of zero and its drop target, because the columns are the process and the process does not disappear when the work does. This is the one thing a regroup over a queryset gets wrong every time.

The board's filter belongs in the URL and the move does not. Somebody sends a colleague a board scoped to Silvassa and this week; nobody sends them a board with one card two columns further along. Write the filter with history.replaceState so a reload keeps the scope, and let the move be what it is — a POST whose answer is the new board.

The snippet root is a bounded frame — h-[640px], rounded-xl, border-zinc-300 — so a whole screen previews in a box. As a real page it is app-shell's main column: drop the height and the border, put h-screen overflow-hidden on the shell, and let the board region take min-h-0 flex-1 so the columns scroll and the page does not.

anatomy.description: The page-header component unchanged: breadcrumb, the one h1, the scope line, and the actions. It does not scroll with the board.

One role="status" on the board root, in the document from first paint, carrying what focus cannot say — the count in the column the card landed in, a refusal and its reason, a rejection from the server.
The single overflow-x-auto box, snap-x, min-h-0 flex-1. The only horizontal scroller in the system and the reason nothing else on the page moves sideways.
A section labelled by its own h2, w-72 and shrink-0, rounded-xl white panel with its own vertical scroller. Never flex-1 — columns that share the width vanish at five stages.
shrink-0: the stage name, the count, the value at that stage, and the limit mark when there is a limit. It stays put while the cards under it scroll.
The ul, bg-zinc-50 — a band recessed inside the white column — holding one li per record. role="list", because Tailwind's reset removes the list semantics with the bullets.
rounded-lg, white, border-zinc-200. One link — the record number — one control, and the two or three facts the decision at that stage needs. No status pill: the column is the status.
The disclosure trigger, named with the record and the stage it is in now, so the announcement after a move is delivered by focus landing on it.
The panel: one full-width button per destination, the current stage absent because it is not a destination, and a refusing stage aria-disabled with its reason on the button.
One line under the facts, an alert-circle in red-600 and a sentence, for a card that is failing on an axis the column does not describe.
The strip under the region carrying the totals across every column. It is the one figure a move does not change.
The count under the h1. On a filtered board it says how many records are on screen out of how many exist, and how many filters are holding the difference.

behaviour: The move control opens the list of destinations inside the card and scrolls the card into view if the panel pushed it below the fold. Escape closes it and returns focus to the control; only one card's panel is open at a time, because the state is on the board.

Choosing a destination moves the card, closes the panel, puts focus on the moved card's move control in its new column and scrolls that column into view. The status region says which stage it went to and how many are there now.

A move in flight leaves the card in the destination with aria-busy and its control aria-disabled. A refusal puts the card back in the column it came from, attaches the reason the server gave and announces it; nothing is silently reverted.

A stage over its limit shows the mark and still accepts cards. A stage that refuses shows its destination button as unavailable with the reason on it, and pressing it announces the refusal rather than doing nothing.
Counts, values and the board total recompute from the cards on every move. The two column totals change and the board total does not.

Drag, where it is offered, calls exactly the same commit as the menu and adds nothing of its own. The column being dragged over shows it is the drop target; a drop outside a column is a no-op, and no card ever ends up nowhere.

Below sm the board stops being columns. The stage becomes a select, one column fills the width, and the counts move into the option labels so the shape of the pipeline is still readable without seeing it.

Filtering never moves a card and never changes a stage. Every column count becomes "4 of 9" and the scope line says how many records are off the board, because on a filtered board an unqualified count is a false statement.

A column with nothing in it keeps its header, its count of zero and its full height, because it is still a destination. A board with nothing on it keeps every column and puts one panel above them saying why.
accessibility: One main, one h1 in the page header, and every column an h2 under it. The heading outline is the pipeline, so a screen reader user can hear the stages in order without reading a card.
Each column is a section named by its own h2 with aria-labelledby, so a landmark or region list reads as the stage names and a card announced out of context still has one.

The card track is a plain list, never a listbox and never a grid. Cards contain a link and a button; a listbox is one Tab stop and nothing inside an option can be reached, which is why list-detail forbids controls on a row and a board requires them.

The move control is named with the record and its current stage — "Move PO-2026-0418, now in With buyer" — so when focus lands on it after a move the new stage is announced by the mechanism that already exists, and the status region is left to carry only what focus cannot.

The status region is on the board root and is in the document before anything moves. It carries the sentences focus cannot deliver: the count in the destination, a refusal and its reason, a rejection from the server. A region rendered with its message already inside it has not changed and announces nothing.
The destination buttons are in a role="group" named "Move <record> to", so the list is announced as a set of destinations rather than as three unrelated buttons in the middle of a card.

A stage that will not accept the card is aria-disabled="true" and stays focusable with the reason written inside the button. The disabled attribute would drop it out of the Tab order, so the one destination somebody is hunting for would be gone with nothing to say why.
A card in flight is aria-busy="true" and its control aria-disabled, so it is not moved twice while the first move is still being decided.
Owner initials in the corner of a card are aria-hidden with the full name in an sr-only span beside them. Two letters in a circle are a picture of a person, not a name.

Drag adds no accessibility of its own and is never the only route. Every draggable card carries the same move control, and the drop handler and the menu call one function, so there is one code path and it is the one the keyboard uses.
